newsitem.title: OMAN: Oman's Sultan to widen consultative process.
newsitem.headline: Oman's Sultan to widen consultative process.

text.p: Oman's Sultan Qaboos bin Said said on Monday his country would set up a State Council to widen the consultative process in the Gulf Arab state.
In a national day speech, he said the State Council "will be a positive body enhancing the constructive cooperation between the government and the people".
"This council will be composed of Omanis, appointed by us, with the experience and capabilities to enrich the consultation process."
Sultan Qaboos in 1991 issued a decree establishing a Shura, or Consultative Council. It is empowered to draft legislation on economic and social matters.
Sultan Qaboos said Oman would move to ease dependence on government expenditure and foreign workers by training Omani nationals to join the work force.
Oman is taking steps towards privatisation and diversification, but analysts say dependence on oil remains a threat to its development.
The government is emphasising a private-sector export-oriented economy.
The government's plan to the year 2000 forecasts annual growth in gross domestic product of 4.6 percent.
Oman signed on Sunday a $2 billion finance agreement with foreign banks and export credit agencies covering downstream work at its $6 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project.
Sultan Qaboos said in his speech that the project would yield substantial returns and fuel future development plans.
Turning to peace in the Middle East, he said that Oman still supported the process, "notwithstanding the obstacles that arise at one time or another".

Oman and Qatar have gone further than their Gulf Arab allies to establish ties with Israel, but businessmen in the oil states say trade flows are still low and some are still wary of dealing openly with the Jewish state.

Sultan Qaboos said "the peace process in itself is an historic work, a noble goal from which it will not be possible to deviate, because of temporary changes in the policies of parties to the problem."
He was apparently referring to the May election of right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
